title: Discord bots as a product surface
metaTitle: Discord bot for community, kept small
excerpt: A Discord bot should live where the community already talks. Design a few commands, help text, and a real way to reach a person.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table. The laptop stands in for a room people already use, where a few commands can sit.
caption: Commands belong where the group already works. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should a community Discord bot live?
faqs.answer: Put it in the server and channel where people already ask repeated questions. Watch a week of that channel before you write commands. A community you hope will arrive after the bot launches is not a surface yet.

faqs.question: How many commands should the bot have?
faqs.answer: A few. Each one needs a name, a small input, a result, and a failure message. Help text lists them in the community's voice. A long menu rots, because every command also needs permissions and a way to recover from a mistake.

faqs.question: Should the bot moderate the server?
faqs.answer: Let it collect a report. Leave removal, conflict, and speaking for moderators to a person, because the community will hold a human responsible for those actions. The path to that person should be a command or a stated channel, not a hope that someone is watching.

markdown:
A Discord bot for community belongs where the community already talks. The bot is a small interface on top of that room: a few commands, help text, and a clear way to reach a human. It is not a second product hidden in a slash menu, and it is not a reason to move a group that lives somewhere else.

Design the commands the way you would design a short screen. Each one does one job, tells the person what happened, and stops.

## Start from the room you have

Name the server, the channel, and the people. A community that already asks for roles, event times, or the latest link in a particular channel has a real surface. A community you hope will appear after the bot launches does not.

Watch a week of the channel before you write commands. The repeated questions are the backlog. If people ask "when is the call" every Tuesday, a command or a pinned reply owned by the bot can answer it. If people are having a conversation that changes every day, leave it. A bot in the middle of an unstructured chat becomes noise.

Decide the channel the bot may speak in. Alerts in a dedicated channel. Commands that answer a person in the channel where the person asked, or in a thread so the main room stays readable. A bot that replies to everything, everywhere, will be muted by the same people you built it for.

## Commands as a small interface

Treat each command as a control with a label, an input, and a result.

- The label is the command name, a verb the community would actually say.
- The input is the minimum the bot needs. A date, a link, a role. Ask for it in the command's prompt, not in a paragraph of rules.
- The result is one message that states what changed or what is true.
- The failure is a second message that says what was missing and how to try again.

Help text is part of the interface, not a README you will write later. `/help` should list the commands in the brand's sentences. A new member should be able to use one command from that list without a tour.

An example, labeled as an exercise: a community server for a product beta. `/office-hours` returns the next session and the link. `/bug` asks for a short description and posts it to a triage channel. `/human` tags the role that is on duty, or tells the person when a person will be back. Three commands, each with a success line and a failure line. That is a surface. A command that "asks the model anything about the product" is a different product, and it needs a source, a limit, and a review before it sits in the same menu.

Permissions are part of the design. Who may open a bug. Who may post an announcement. Who may configure the bot. A community bot that lets every member broadcast will be used that way once, and then the moderators will turn it off.

## Help text and the path to a person

Write the empty and error states with the same care as the happy command. If someone types a command the bot does not have, say so, and show the short list. If a command is temporarily unavailable, say that, and say how to reach a person. Silence reads as a broken room.

The path to a human should be a command or a stated channel, not a hope that someone is watching. "Talk to a moderator in #help" is a design. "Someone will probably see this" is not.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) organize guidelines under four principles, including operable and understandable, and note that WCAG can also be applied to software. A command menu is operable when people can discover it and recover from a mistake. A reply is understandable when it states the outcome in ordinary words. Emoji can support a status. Emoji cannot be the only status.

Keep the bot's voice inside the community's voice. If the server is plain and specific, the bot should be plain and specific. A character with a catchphrase gets old in the second week and makes serious alerts harder to trust.

## What not to automate in the room

Do not automate moderation judgment on day one. Removing a person, or speaking for the moderators in a conflict, is the kind of action the community will hold a human responsible for. A bot can collect a report. A person decides.

Do not mirror the entire product into Discord. If the product is a dashboard, link to the dashboard. The bot can notify that something changed. The bot should not become a worse copy of the screen, rebuilt out of messages.

Do not add a command because the API makes it easy. Every command is a promise that help text, permissions, and failure states will be kept. A menu of twenty promises will rot. A menu of three will be used.

Review the bot the way you review a screen. Once a month, read the help text against the commands that still work, and delete anything the community did not use. An unused command is not free. It is a wrong door in a short menu, and new members will try it.

Hanabi builds Discord bots when the community and the commands are this specific. The craft is the same as a small interface: few actions, obvious results, a way out when the script ends.

## If the group is not here

Some teams live in Telegram instead, with a known group and the same need for status, intake, and alerts. The room changes. The rule does not. That companion is [what a Telegram bot is good for](/blog/what-a-telegram-bot-is-good-for).

Choose the room by where people already are. Building in the other app, and then asking the community to move, spends the trust the bot needed in order to be useful.

If the commands are clear enough to design, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio can shape the small surface and build it where the community talks.
